headline: Highest risk is prompt-injection and cascading-error from pairing a shell-capable container tool with a prompt-leakage corpus; other risks are lower due to limited shared surfaces.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can read files and execute shell commands, while agent_b is a prompt-leakage corpus with no isolation or provenance controls shown. The pair has no documented shared channel, but if agent_a ingests agent_b content as instructions, injection is plausible. Uncertainty about the bridge pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a is configured to read agent_b-produced text as instructions, injection becomes actionable.
IF a shared filesystem or copy-paste bridge is introduced, attacker-controlled content can steer agent_a.
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction-following from external text.
Require provenance labels on any content passed from agent_b to agent_a.
Use a read-only handoff file with a fixed schema.
Add a manual review step before agent_a executes commands from agent_b output.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches filesystem artifacts, certificate private keys, and registry credentials, but agent_b has network_egress none and no file or workspace access is documented. Without a shared workspace or upload path, leakage is not established; the main risk is accidental manual transfer, which is small-burst.
conditions: IF a shared workspace is mounted between the agents, sensitive files from agent_a can be exposed to agent_b.
IF operator copies agent_a outputs into agent_b prompts, secrets may be disclosed.
mitigations: Keep separate workspaces and mounts.
Redact secrets before any handoff.
Block outbound network from any process that can read agent_a artifacts.
Review logs for accidental secret inclusion.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, but agent_b exposes no write or filesystem capabilities. There is no documented shared mutable resource, so direct write-write conflict is not shown. Uncertainty remains because agent_b's operational surface is sparse, so low is the safest non-zero choice.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory, file clobbering becomes possible.
IF an orchestrator later grants agent_b write access, conflicts can emerge.
mitigations: Assign distinct working directories.
Mount shared inputs read-only.
Serialize any writes through one coordinator.
Add file-locking for shared artifacts.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate container-analysis outputs from files and commands, and agent_b appears to be a prompt-leakage-oriented agent that may render or reuse text. If agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream outputs. No verification step is documented, so medium fits the default-pathway risk.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without verification, incorrect findings can propagate.
IF agent_a outputs malformed or adversarial text, agent_b may reproduce it.
mitigations: Insert a verification step before reuse of agent_a output.
Require citations for any factual claim passed onward.
Limit agent_b to summarization, not action-taking.
Flag low-confidence statements for human review.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a explicitly handles certificate private keys, registry credentials, and vulnerability data, while agent_b has no documented compliance controls, residency, or retention policy. That mismatch creates a plausible compliance gap if the pair processes regulated or secret material. Because only agent_a shows sensitive-data handling, the other agent is cited only for missing controls.
conditions: IF regulated secrets or customer data are routed through agent_b, retention and residency obligations may be unmet.
IF logs from either agent retain sensitive artifacts, deletion/export obligations may fail.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from agent_b inputs.
Set short log retention and verify deletion.
Document data residency for any shared workflow.
Run a quick compliance review before deployment.
